Bermuda Imposes Broad Tariffs on Imports, Disrupting Key Sectors

HAMILTON, Bermuda — The Bermudian government’s sweeping new tariff regime on imported goods took effect Friday, sparking widespread concerns across the island’s business community and hitting sectors ranging from automotive to construction and food retail.

The broad-based tariffs, announced unexpectedly earlier in the week, apply to a wide array of imported products, with duties rising by as much as 25% in some categories. Government officials said the measures are aimed at curbing the territory’s trade deficit and boosting local industry, though critics warned of rising prices and supply disruptions.

Brilliance China Automotive Holdings Ltd, a key supplier of vehicles to Bermudian dealerships, was among the first companies to confirm shipment delays and increased costs as a result of the new tariffs. “We are assessing the immediate operational impact and are in active discussions with our partners in Bermuda,” a company spokesperson said in a statement. “Our priority is to minimize disruption to customers.”

Automotive dealers reported that new vehicle shipments were already being held at the port while importers renegotiate contracts and assess the higher duties. “We’re seeing price hikes of 10 to 20 percent on new cars overnight. It’s not just luxury vehicles—it’s every model we bring in,” said Thomas Edgerton, general manager of Island Motors Ltd.

The tariffs extend to building materials, electronics, packaged foods, and household goods, prompting fears of inflation. The Bermuda Chamber of Commerce issued a statement saying, “While we recognize the government’s fiscal concerns, the scale of these tariffs will mean higher costs for businesses and families across the island. We urge authorities to reconsider the breadth of these measures.”

At Hamilton’s main supermarket, customers expressed frustration at the sudden jump in prices. “I just paid nearly double for olive oil and pasta compared to last week,” said local resident Marcia Landy. “It’s a shock to a lot of us.”

Finance Minister Richard Swan defended the move, saying the tariffs are designed to encourage local alternatives and reduce Bermuda’s dependence on overseas suppliers. “We are taking decisive action in the best long-term interests of our economy,” Swan told reporters. “We understand there will be short-term adjustments.”

Analysts said the full impact remains unclear as importers and retailers grapple with the new rules. “We could see supply chain bottlenecks in the coming weeks,” said Alicia Greaves, an economist at the Bermuda Policy Institute. “The question is whether local producers can fill the gap, especially in specialized goods.”

The government said it would review the tariff structure after 90 days.
